newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council delays decision on Sudan air embargo.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council delays decision on Sudan air embargo.

text.p: The Security Council on Thursday delayed for a month a decision on implementing an air embargo against Sudan for failing to extradite three men wanted for an attempt to kill Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak last year, council members said.
The council decided in mid-August to impose the air ban but postponed setting a date for its entry into force for at least 90 days, pending a report from Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Sudan is already the target of mandatory diplomatic and travel sanctions that went into effect on May 10 after a two-week grace period.
The secretary-general's report, circulated this week and based on the findings of a U.N. special envoy, former Algerian Foreign Minister Lakhdar Brahimi, showed no change in the situation.

Sudan continued to maintain it had no trace of the three men wanted for involvement in a plot to assassinate Mubarak after he arrived in Addis Ababa on June 26, 1995, for a summit of the Organisation of African Unity. It also denied supporting or facilitating any terrorist activities.

When the council discussed the report during private consultations on Thursday, France called for a 30-day delay in deciding on a date for the air embargo, to allow time for a report on the humanitarian impact of the new measures, diplomats said.
This was supported by Russia and Egypt, whose lead on the Sudan issue is usually followed by other council members.
Sudan says an air embargo would have dire humanitarian effects, such as preventing imports of medicines and travel by thousands of Sudanese seeking medical treatment abroad.

The air embargo decided in principle in August would require all countries to deny permission to aircraft registered in Sudan, or leased or operated by Sudan Airways or the Sudanese government, to take off from, land in or overfly their territory.

The sanctions against Sudan in effect since May require U.N. members to reduce the number and level of their diplomatic staffs in that country and to restrict entry into or through their territory of members of Sudan's government, civil service and armed forces.
